variants.title: Cross the five boundaries
variants.context: One text-to-image request crosses five model boundaries: tokenize and encode the prompt, create noisy latents from a recorded seed, predict a cleaner state with the denoiser, apply the scheduler update, then decode and inspect the pixels.
variants.prompt: A user submits a prompt with no reference image. Put the pipeline stages in order.

items.text: Predict a cleaner state with the denoiser while attending to the timestep and the conditioning.
Decode the final latent into pixels and evaluate the actual image before release.
Initialize a noisy latent from the recorded seed and the requested dimensions.
Tokenize the prompt and encode it into contextual vectors with the pinned text encoder.
Apply the scheduler so that prediction becomes the next, slightly cleaner sample.

variants.hint: Which stage decides what conditioning ever reaches the image model?
variants.explanation: The outer pipeline is stable even when the denoiser backbone, sampler, or conditioning method changes.

variants.title: Cross the five boundaries
variants.context: One text-to-image request crosses five model boundaries: tokenize and encode the prompt, create noisy latents from a recorded seed, predict a cleaner state with the denoiser, apply the scheduler update, then decode and inspect the pixels.
variants.prompt: The request adds a depth map as a structural control alongside the prompt. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Sample the starting latent from the recorded seed.
Let the denoiser attend to the timestep, the text signal, and the structural signal at each step.
Let the scheduler turn every prediction into the next state across the timestep schedule.
Decode the final latent and check whether the structure conflicts with the requested text.
Encode the prompt text and preprocess the depth map into its conditioning form.

variants.hint: A structural control joins the conditioning, it does not replace the sampling loop.
variants.explanation: Image-derived controls such as edges, depth, segmentation, or pose enter as conditioning; excessive strength can make the result rigid or fight the prompt.

variants.title: Cross the five boundaries
variants.context: One text-to-image request crosses five model boundaries: tokenize and encode the prompt, create noisy latents from a recorded seed, predict a cleaner state with the denoiser, apply the scheduler update, then decode and inspect the pixels.
variants.prompt: A trace shows the job spent most of its wall clock before any model call. Put the recorded stage timings in the order they occur.

items.text: Denoising: the sequential sampling loop spends its steps.
Encoding: the normalized prompt becomes conditioning vectors.
Queueing: the job waits for a worker holding the pinned recipe.
Evaluation: the candidate is inspected against quality and policy checks.
Decoding: the final latent becomes pixels.
Storage: the accepted image and its trace are written.

variants.hint: A useful trace records more than the seed.
variants.explanation: Stage timings for queueing, encoding, denoising, decoding, evaluation, and storage are what let you attribute latency instead of guessing at it.

variants.title: Gate the release path
variants.context: Prompt filtering and output filtering protect different boundaries. Requests are classified before compute, candidates stay private until required checks finish, the actual pixels are inspected, and only then is the result released with recorded context.
variants.prompt: A routine request is generated and released. Put the safety steps in order.

items.text: Record the decision, attach supported provenance, and release with the appropriate labeling.
Apply content, identity, privacy, and product checks to the image that was actually generated.
Authenticate the caller, enforce product scope, and inspect the prompt and reference inputs before scheduling GPU time.
Run the pinned model recipe and keep the candidate private.

variants.hint: Which check can run before any GPU time is bought?
variants.explanation: Prompt filtering and output filtering protect different boundaries, so both run and the candidate stays private in between.

variants.title: Gate the release path
variants.context: Prompt filtering and output filtering protect different boundaries. Requests are classified before compute, candidates stay private until required checks finish, the actual pixels are inspected, and only then is the result released with recorded context.
variants.prompt: A permitted prompt produces a candidate that violates the identity policy. Put the steps in order, ending where the candidate stops.

items.text: The decision, policy version, and review route are recorded instead of a release.
Output inspection finds an identity violation in the actual pixels.
The prompt gate finds nothing prohibited and the job is scheduled.
The pinned recipe generates a candidate that is not published yet.

variants.hint: A permitted prompt can still produce a disallowed candidate.
variants.explanation: Output inspection exists because the prompt gate cannot determine everything a stochastic model will render.

variants.title: Gate the release path
variants.context: Prompt filtering and output filtering protect different boundaries. Requests are classified before compute, candidates stay private until required checks finish, the actual pixels are inspected, and only then is the result released with recorded context.
variants.prompt: A request is clearly outside the product's scope. Put the steps in order, ending before GPU time is spent.

items.text: Reject the request before scheduling GPU time.
Inspect the prompt and any reference inputs against the request policy.
Record the rejection with its policy version so an appeal can be reviewed.
Authenticate the caller and load the product scope and policy version.

variants.hint: Rejecting early saves compute, but only if the reason is recorded.
variants.explanation: Clearly prohibited work is rejected before GPU scheduling, while an overbroad prompt rule risks rejecting harmless requests before any evidence exists.

variants.title: Budget the job time
variants.context: For one measured deployment profile a first planning approximation is job time equals fixed overhead plus denoising steps times the measured time per step. Resolution, guidance implementation, batching, precision, and hardware all change that per-step measurement.
variants.prompt: A measured profile shows 1.2 seconds of fixed overhead and 0.09 seconds per denoising step. A job runs 30 steps. What is the planned job time?
variants.hint: The overhead is a per-job constant, not a per-step one.
variants.explanation: Job time is fixed overhead plus steps times the measured per-step time, so the sequential loop is the part that grows with the step count.

mistakes.feedback: You dropped the fixed overhead, which is added once per job.
You charged the fixed overhead to every step instead of once.

variants.title: Budget the job time
variants.context: For one measured deployment profile a first planning approximation is job time equals fixed overhead plus denoising steps times the measured time per step. Resolution, guidance implementation, batching, precision, and hardware all change that per-step measurement.
variants.prompt: A profile measures 1.5 seconds of fixed overhead and 0.075 seconds per step. One observed job took 6.0 seconds. How many denoising steps did it run?
variants.explanation: Only the denoising portion scales with steps, so subtract the fixed overhead first and then divide by the measured per-step time.

mistakes.feedback: You divided the whole job time by the per-step time without removing the fixed overhead.
You added the overhead instead of subtracting it before dividing.

variants.title: Budget the job time
variants.context: For one measured deployment profile a first planning approximation is job time equals fixed overhead plus denoising steps times the measured time per step. Resolution, guidance implementation, batching, precision, and hardware all change that per-step measurement.
variants.prompt: A profile has 1.0 second of fixed overhead and 0.08 seconds per step. A distilled recipe cuts a job from 50 steps to 20 at the same overhead and per-step cost. By how many seconds does the job time fall?
variants.hint: The overhead is paid in both versions, so it cancels.
variants.explanation: Only the sequential denoising work changes, so the saving is the removed steps times the measured per-step time.

mistakes.feedback: That is the new job time, not the reduction.
You compared the old job time against the new denoising time and forgot the overhead in the new job.

variants.title: Diagnose the stage
variants.context: A latent pipeline can lose information in the denoising loop, in the decoder, or in both. Fine text, tiny objects, sharp boundaries, and repeated patterns are the usual casualties, so diagnose the stage before tuning prompt wording.
variants.prompt: Across many seeds the composition and object placement are correct, but thin repeated patterns smear and sharp boundaries soften at the product resolution. Where should the team look first?
options: The prompt wording, since the pattern description is probably too vague to follow.
The seed policy, since a different starting state would sharpen those boundaries.
The latent decoder, since the composition formed but the reconstruction loses fine detail.
optionFeedback: Wrong: wording would change composition too, and the composition is already correct across seeds.
Wrong: a failure that repeats across many seeds is not caused by one starting state.
Correct: the decoder reconstructs pixels from the final latent and cannot add detail the compressed state dropped.
variants.hint: Which stage reconstructs pixels rather than composing them?
variants.explanation: The decoder does not repair a composition the denoising loop never formed, and compression can lose fine detail, so diagnose the stage before rewriting the prompt.

variants.title: Diagnose the stage
variants.context: A latent pipeline can lose information in the denoising loop, in the decoder, or in both. Fine text, tiny objects, sharp boundaries, and repeated patterns are the usual casualties, so diagnose the stage before tuning prompt wording.
variants.prompt: A team raises classifier-free guidance well above its evaluated range. Alignment rises slightly, but images oversaturate and every seed returns the same composition. What is the correct reading?
options: Guidance traded diversity and artifact control for prompt adherence and is now past its useful range.
The denoiser is undertrained, because a well-trained model tolerates any guidance value.
The scheduler is wrong, because guidance only changes how the prompt is encoded.
optionFeedback: Correct: raising guidance pushes the sample toward the prompt signal while reducing variation and amplifying artifacts.
Wrong: the useful guidance range is model and workload specific for every model, however well trained.
Wrong: guidance combines an unconditional and a conditioned prediction; it does not change text encoding.
variants.hint: Guidance is a trade-off, not a universal quality dial.
variants.explanation: Classifier-free guidance trades fidelity against diversity, so the useful range has to be measured per model and workload rather than assumed.

variants.title: Diagnose the stage
variants.context: A latent pipeline can lose information in the denoising loop, in the decoder, or in both. Fine text, tiny objects, sharp boundaries, and repeated patterns are the usual casualties, so diagnose the stage before tuning prompt wording.
variants.prompt: A support case says the same seed and prompt produced different pixels after the fleet moved to new GPUs and a lower precision. What should the response be?
options: The seed was never actually recorded, because a recorded seed guarantees identical pixels.
Sampling is random by design, so no configuration can make two runs comparable.
A seed fixes the starting state for one implementation, so the whole recipe must match to compare pixels.
optionFeedback: Wrong: a seed controls the sampled starting state, not every numeric detail downstream of it.
Wrong: a fixed recipe plus a fixed seed does support comparison within one implementation.
Correct: models, runtimes, precision, and hardware are part of what makes an output reproducible.
variants.hint: What else besides the seed decides the trajectory?
variants.explanation: A seed controls the sampled starting state for a given implementation; changed models, runtimes, precision, or hardware can change the output.

variants.title: Sort the evidence
variants.context: No single automatic metric proves a text-to-image model is useful. Prompt alignment asks whether the request was followed, visual quality asks whether the image is coherent, diversity asks whether the model covers the task, and safety and rights asks whether the candidate may be released.
variants.prompt: A release suite lists four checks. Match each evaluation dimension with the check that belongs to it.

pairs.label: Prompt alignment
pairs.detail: Count the requested objects and check left-right relations and omitted attributes.

pairs.label: Visual quality
pairs.detail: Inspect hands, edges, and decoder artifacts at the product's actual resolution.

pairs.label: Diversity
pairs.detail: Compare several seeds and paraphrases for repeated composition or missing modes.

pairs.label: Safety and rights
pairs.detail: Measure policy misses and false positives by content class and language.

variants.hint: Ask what a failure in each row would look like to a user.
variants.explanation: Aggregate similarity can hide binding errors, so the four dimensions are measured separately rather than averaged into one score.

variants.title: Sort the evidence
variants.context: No single automatic metric proves a text-to-image model is useful. Prompt alignment asks whether the request was followed, visual quality asks whether the image is coherent, diversity asks whether the model covers the task, and safety and rights asks whether the candidate may be released.
variants.prompt: Four failures arrive from a canary. Match each evaluation dimension with the failure it belongs to.

pairs.label: Prompt alignment
pairs.detail: A prompt asking for three red chairs returns four, two of them blue.

pairs.label: Visual quality
pairs.detail: Typography in a rendered sign looks fine as a thumbnail and garbled at full size.

pairs.label: Diversity
pairs.detail: Ten seeds for one prompt return the same camera angle and background.

pairs.label: Safety and rights
pairs.detail: A benign look-alike prompt is blocked in one language and allowed in another.

variants.hint: One of these is a false positive rather than a missed hazard.
variants.explanation: Slices are built before averaging, so counts, typography, seed variation, and language each get their own evidence.

variants.title: Sort the evidence
variants.context: No single automatic metric proves a text-to-image model is useful. Prompt alignment asks whether the request was followed, visual quality asks whether the image is coherent, diversity asks whether the model covers the task, and safety and rights asks whether the candidate may be released.
variants.prompt: Four observations come from a review of production samples. Match each evaluation dimension with the observation it belongs to.

pairs.label: Prompt alignment
pairs.detail: The requested item sits above the shelf when the prompt asked for below it.

pairs.label: Visual quality
pairs.detail: Compression halos appear along high-contrast edges after decoding.

pairs.label: Diversity
pairs.detail: Average quality is high while every paraphrase collapses to one composition.

pairs.label: Safety and rights
pairs.detail: The policy detector was unavailable and the candidate has no recorded decision.

variants.hint: High average quality can coexist with a missing mode.
variants.explanation: Spatial relations, decoder artifacts, mode coverage, and policy evidence are different failures, and only slice-level evidence separates them.
